name: LMC7660IMX_NOPB
title: LMC7660 switched-capacitor voltage converter
summary: A CMOS charge-pump inverter: from a +1.5 V to +10 V supply it makes the matching negative rail, −1.5 V to −10 V, using only an external pump capacitor and an output reservoir. An internal oscillator of about 10 kHz, divided by two, drives four MOS switches. It needs no output diode anywhere in its supply and temperature range and fits the sockets of 7660 designs. LMC7660IMX/NOPB is the SOIC-8 part on a 2500-piece reel, rated −40 °C to 85 °C.

circuits.title: Figure 1. Test circuit
circuits.description: The circuit the electrical characteristics are measured in: a 5 V supply inverted to about −5 V, with a 10 µF pump capacitor across CAP+ and CAP− and a 10 µF reservoir on the output. The load RL hangs between V+ and the output, so the supply current IS splits into the load current IL and the chip's own draw. A switch connects LV to ground for low-voltage tests, and an optional capacitor from OSC to ground slows the oscillator.

parts.note: optional, dashed; zero for the table's figures

circuits.title: Figure 12. Lower supply current with a slower oscillator
circuits.description: The basic inverter with a capacitor Cosc added between V+ and OSC. The extra capacitance pulls the oscillator down from about 10 kHz towards a few hundred hertz (Figure 2), and the supply current falls with it. A switch connects LV to ground; LV is grounded only with V+ at or below 3.5 V.

circuits.title: Figure 13. Running from an external clock
circuits.description: A CMOS gate with its inputs tied drives OSC through 1 kΩ, overriding the internal RC oscillator with an outside clock. The clock still passes the internal divide-by-two, so the capacitors are pumped at half the clock frequency. LV is left open.

parts.note: both inputs tied to the clock

circuits.title: Figure 14. Two converters in parallel for lower output resistance
circuits.description: Two LMC7660s share the supply, ground and one 10 µF reservoir on their joined outputs; each keeps its own 10 µF pump capacitor. The combined output resistance is one device's Rout divided by the number of devices.

circuits.title: Figure 15. Two converters cascaded for −2V+
circuits.description: The first LMC7660 makes −V+. The second takes ground as its supply pin and the first stage's output as its ground pin, so it inverts again below −V+ and gives −2V+. Currents marked with a load IL: IL at the output and into the second device's V+ pin, 2IL from the first stage's output into the second device's GND pin and into the first device's V+ pin, 4IL at the first device's GND pin. Each stage draws twice its load current, and output resistance is roughly the sum of the two stages' Rout.

circuits.title: Figure 16. −15 V from +5 V
circuits.description: The cascade of Figure 15 with the second device's V+ pin returned to +5 V instead of ground. Its ground pin sits on the first stage's −5 V, so it works across 10 V and inverts that below −5 V, giving −15 V. The second LMC7660 then spans the full 20 V between +5 V and −15 V, so the input must stay at +5 V.

circuits.title: Figure 17. Half-supply splitter
circuits.description: A divider that holds a node at exactly V+/2 for light loads, such as a mid-supply point from a battery. Two 100 µF capacitors alternate between series across the supply and parallel with each other, which forces equal voltage on both. The GND pin is the V+/2 output, VOUT goes to ground and LV goes to ground through 1 MΩ. Each switch sees only V+/2, so the supply may go to 20 V for a 10 V output.

circuits.title: Figure 18. Positive voltage doubler
circuits.description: Two diodes turn the converter into a positive multiplier. While CAP+ is low, the 10 µF pump capacitor charges from V+ through D1. When CAP+ swings up to V+, the capacitor's top is lifted to about 2V+ less a diode drop and charges the 10 µF output reservoir through D2. The output is 2V+ − 2VD. Only CAP+ is used; CAP− is left open and VOUT is grounded.

circuits.title: Figure 19. Negative converter and positive doubler together
circuits.description: Figure 18's doubler on CAP+ with the usual inverter on the other two switches, so one chip gives both 2V+ − 2VD and −V+. CP1 pumps the diode junction above V+ while CP2 and CR2 make the negative output; all four capacitors are 10 µF.
notes: Misprint: CR2's + terminal should be at ground, as for the output reservoir in Figure 1.

circuits.title: Figure 20. Micropower thermometer, −55 °C to +125 °C, 150 µA
circuits.description: Figure 19's dual converter run from two 1.5 V cells powers an LM35 temperature sensor. The doubled positive rail feeds the sensor, and the negative rail pulls its output down through 47 kΩ so it can go below zero for temperatures under 0 °C. The output reads 10 mV/°C over −55 °C to +125 °C, and the whole circuit draws about 150 µA. LV is grounded. All capacitors are 20 µF.

circuits.title: Figure 21. Regulated −5 V, 200 µA standby
circuits.description: An LP2951 regulator closes a loop round the LMC7660 to hold the output at −5 V. The LP2951 runs between the input and the regulated negative output (its pin 4) and feeds the converter's V+ from its pin 1, with pins 6 and 7 joined and 0.022 µF from pin 1 to pin 7. The output holds −5 V at 10 mA from a 6 V input, and up to 25 mA from inputs above 7 V. Pin 5 is an error flag pulled up by 330 kΩ that goes low when the output falls about 5 %; taking pin 3 high shuts the regulator down.

circuits.title: Figure 22. Adjustable negative regulator
circuits.description: Figure 21 with the LP2951's feedback pin 7 taken from a divider instead of from its pin 6: R2 from the regulated output to pin 7 and R1 from pin 7 to ground; LP2951 pins 2 and 6 have no connection. The output can then be set anywhere from −2.0 V to −10 V by Vout = Vref (1 + R1/R2) with Vref = 1.235 V. A link from LV to ground is optional, for low-voltage operation.
notes: LV may be linked to ground (a dotted connection) for low-voltage operation; open otherwise.

operation.text: Four large CMOS switches alternate in two phases. In the first, S1 and S3 close and Cp charges to V+ between V+ and ground. In the second, S2 and S4 close: S2 puts Cp's positive side on ground, so its negative side, through S4, drives the reservoir Cr below ground. Over many cycles Cr settles at exactly −V+ when there is no load and the switches are lossless.

S1 is P-channel; S2, S3 and S4 are N-channel. Since the output lies below ground, substrate logic biases the p− wells of S3 and S4 so that they never forward-bias against their sources or drains, and holds the S4 well at the most negative potential in the circuit. The level translator takes its supply from that well, which lets it turn S4 off with VGS4 = 0.

An internal RC oscillator followed by a divide-by-two times the switches through the level translator; the pump runs at half the oscillator frequency. An internal regulator feeds the divider and oscillator, saving power at high supply voltage, and comes in near V+ = 6.5 V. With V+ at or below 3.5 V, grounding LV improves low-voltage operation; at 3.5 V and above LV must be open to avoid damaging the part.

Three things set how close efficiency comes to 100 %: the power taken by the switch drive, the matching and on-resistance of the switches, and the impedance of Cp and Cr at the pump rate. The LMC7660 keeps the first two small; the third depends on the capacitors fitted. With a large Cp each transfer takes only a small part of its charge, so its voltage moves little and little energy is lost (equation 1).
Ripple falls as the reservoir Cr grows. For a 5 mA load and 200 mV of ripple at the 10 kHz oscillator, about 10 µF is needed (equation 2).

Stay within the maximum supply voltage and junction temperature. Do not ground LV (pin 6) with a supply above 3.5 V. Never short the output to V+. Fit the electrolytic Cp and Cr with the polarity of Figure 1: Cp positive at CAP+, Cr positive at ground.

Older 7660 parts needed a series output diode at high temperature or supply voltage to prevent destructive latch-up, at a cost in output voltage and series resistance. The LMC7660 needs no output diode anywhere in its supply and temperature range, and also works with the diode Dx left in an existing design.

A capacitor Cosc on OSC (Figure 12) brings the oscillator down from its nominal 10 kHz to a few hundred hertz, and the supply current down into the 10 µA region, which suits micropower and battery back-up use. At the lower pump rate Cp and Cr look like higher impedances; larger values recover the ripple and load current needed.

A CMOS gate driving OSC through 1 kΩ (Figure 13) overrides the internal oscillator, to run faster or to keep switching noise away from sensitive frequencies. The divide-by-two still acts, so the pump frequency is half the clock frequency.
Several LMC7660s in parallel lower the output resistance in proportion to their number. Each needs its own Cp; one Cr serves them all (Figure 14).

Stacked converters give larger negative voltages (Figure 15). Each stage draws twice the current it delivers, and the output resistances roughly add, so only a few stages are practical. Returning the second device's V+ to +5 V instead of ground gives −15 V from +5 V (Figure 16); that device then sees 20 V, so the input must not exceed +5 V.

In Figure 17 the capacitors are in series across the supply during one half cycle and in parallel during the other, so charge shares out until each holds exactly V+/2. It serves as a precise divider for light loads or a mid-supply point for batteries. Every switch sees only V+/2, which lets the supply rise to 20 V for a 10 V output.

With two diodes the part doubles (Figure 18). In one half cycle S2 grounds the negative side of Cp1 and it charges to V+ − VD1 through D1, with D2 off. In the other, S1 lifts that side to V+, putting the diode junction at V+ + (V+ − VD1) and charging the output through D2 while D1 is off. The doubler needs just S1 and S2; the other two can run an inverter at the same time (Figure 19).

Figure 19's dual converter on two 1.5 V cells runs an LM35 sensor (10 mV/°C, 50 µA quiescent) whose output is pulled to the negative rail so it can read below zero; the circuit covers −55 °C to +125 °C and draws about 150 µA. Schottky diodes in the up-converter stretch battery life.

Placing the LMC7660 inside an LP2951's loop regulates the output and keeps micropower operation (Figure 21): −5 V at 10 mA with a 6 V input, and in regulation to 25 mA with inputs above 7 V. The LP2951's error flag (pin 5) goes low when the output (pin 4) drops about 5 %; its pin 3 taken high shuts it down. The LMC7660 itself stops when pin 7 is joined to pin 8. With an external divider on the LP2951 (Figure 22) the output can be set from −2.0 V to −10 V.
